knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.6)
library(paweh)
```

# Should we sequence more deeply or recruit more people?

A team has funding to sequence DNA for a genetic association study. If it
pays for more reads per participant, it may have fewer people to recruit.
Would four reads at a variant site provide enough information, or would a
deeper design give the study a better chance of detecting the proposed
effect?

DNA sequencing measures the order of bases in pieces of DNA. A **read** is
one such sequence of base calls. A read covering a variant site gives one
observation of the base at that position. **Depth**, or coverage, counts
those observations. In the fixed-depth examples here, 4×, 10× and 25× mean
exactly 4, 10 and 25 reads at the site for a person with that depth.

We consider a site with two possible alleles, reference and alternate. A
person carries two copies, one inherited from each parent. The **genotype**
is coded 0, 1 or 2 according to the number of alternate copies. A base-call
error occurs when a read reports the wrong allele, for example because of
noise in measuring the sequencing signal. A genotype-call error occurs
when the genotype inferred from all the reads differs from the person's
true genotype. How often that happens depends on how many reads sampled
each copy as well as on the accuracy of each read.

The diagram follows a person carrying one copy of each allele. Each square
is a possible read at the same site. Both rows illustrate accurate base calls.

```{r read-sampling, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Two possible read patterns from the same heterozygous genotype. R denotes reference and A denotes alternate.", fig.alt="At depth four all reads show R. At depth ten, five reads show R and five show A."}
par(mar = rep(0.3, 4))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(-2.2, 10.7), ylim = c(0, 3.7), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
reads <- function(y, bases, label) {
  x <- seq_along(bases)
  rect(x - .41, y - .32, x + .41, y + .32, border = "#374853",
       col = ifelse(bases == "R", "#d3eaf2", "#f8dcb4"))
  text(x, y, bases, font = 2)
  text(-1.8, y, label, adj = 0, font = 2)
}
text(-1.8, 3.29, "True genotype: R / A", adj = 0, font = 2)
reads(2.45, rep("R", 4), "4 reads")
text(.59, 1.94, "Only one allele appears in this sample.", adj = 0, cex = .88)
reads(1.12, c("R","A","A","R","A","R","R","A","R","A"), "10 reads")
text(.59, .60, "Both alleles appear in this sample.", adj = 0, cex = .88)
```

With four independently sampled reads from a heterozygote, all four can
come from the same allele by chance. With ten reads there are more
opportunities to see both copies. These drawings illustrate possible
outcomes. The calculations below sum the probabilities of the possible
read counts.

## What happens with perfectly accurate reads?

Set the per-read error probability to zero and compare two depths. Each
row of the matrix below starts from a known true genotype. Read across
the row to see the probabilities of the three possible calls.

```{r zero-error-matrices}
list(
  coverage_2 = ngs_genotype_error_matrix(2, 0),
  coverage_10 = ngs_genotype_error_matrix(10, 0)
)
```

At 2×, a true heterozygote is called 0, 1 or 2 with probabilities 0.25,
0.50 and 0.25. At 10× its probability of a correct call is 0.99805.
For depth \(v\), the chance that every read comes from the same copy is
\(2(1/2)^v\) in this model. That remaining sampling uncertainty explains
why setting base-call error to zero still leaves some wrong genotype calls.

# Choose the design by what is sampled

If the team recruits unrelated cases and controls, it can compare genotype
scores across the two groups. If it recruits affected children with both
parents, it can ask which allele a parent transmitted to the affected child.
The diagram follows the same kind of read evidence through each analysis.

```{r workflow-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Two ways to use reads at one biallelic site. Each column ends in a recruitment target with different units.", fig.alt="Unrelated cases and controls yield called genotype distributions and a trend test. Complete families yield a trio read-count likelihood and a transmission test."}
par(mar = rep(.35, 4))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 8), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
path <- function(x, title, steps, fill) {
  text(x, 7.6, title, font = 2)
  y <- c(6.3, 4.55, 2.8, 1.05)
  for (i in seq_along(y)) {
    rect(x-2.25, y[i]-.57, x+2.25, y[i]+.57, col=fill, border="#425561")
    text(x, y[i], steps[i], cex=.91)
    if (i < length(y)) arrows(x,y[i]-.63,x,y[i+1]+.64,length=.09)
  }
}
path(2.5, "Case-control NGS",
     c("Reads in unrelated\ncases and controls", "Probability of each\ngenotype call",
       "Compare mean genotype scores\nbetween groups", "Recruit cases and controls"),
     "#e2f0f5")
path(7.5, "TDT1-NGS",
     c("Reads in two parents\nand their affected child", "Likelihood across possible\nfamily genotypes",
       "Assess preferential\ntransmission", "Recruit complete trios"),
     "#e3f0e6")
```

One poor genotype call can move a case or control into the wrong score
category. In the family design, uncertain genotypes can still contribute
evidence through the probabilities of the observed read counts. The two
methods therefore answer different sampling questions. Both take proposed
design parameters as inputs. FASTQ, BAM and VCF processing and tests on
individual records are outside these prospective calculations.

A few quantities recur throughout the examples:

- **Allele frequency** is the fraction of allele copies of a particular
  type in the source population. The **minor allele frequency** (MAF) is
  the frequency of the less common allele. The argument `pd` refers to
  the designated risk allele, which can be either allele.
- **Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium** (HWE) supplies expected genotype
  proportions. With risk-allele frequency \(p\), these are
  \((1-p)^2, 2p(1-p), p^2\) for zero, one and two copies under random
  pairing of alleles. The trio examples also assume independent parental
  genotypes under random mating.
- **Relative risk** compares disease probabilities. If disease risks are
  \(u\) and \(v\) in two groups, their risk ratio is \(u/v\). An
  **odds ratio** (OR) compares \(u/(1-u)\) with \(v/(1-v)\). Converting
  between them generally requires a baseline risk.
- **Linkage disequilibrium** (LD) means alleles at two sites occur together
  on chromosomes more or less often than their separate frequencies predict.
  A marker in LD with a disease allele can show an association even if the
  marker itself has no effect.
- **Power** is the chance of rejecting the null hypothesis under the
  proposed association. The **significance level**, `alpha`, specifies
  the nominal false-positive probability under the null. The minimum sample
  size needed (MSSN) answers the inverse question for a target power.

# Affected-child trios: how much sequencing does a family need?

In a **complete trio**, both biological parents and their affected child
provide DNA. A parent who carries both alleles could have transmitted
either one. The transmission disequilibrium test (TDT) asks whether one
allele is transmitted more often than expected to affected children. At low
depth it can be unclear which genotypes the three people carry. Kim's
TDT1-NGS uses the read counts in the whole family to weigh each possible
Mendelian inheritance pattern.

## Kim's adolescent idiopathic scoliosis example

Kim (2015) asked how many trios would give adequate power in an adolescent
idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) design. For the marker rs1400180 the planning
frequency was 0.35. The study assumed symmetric per-read error of 0.025,
equal depth for each family member and a genome-wide threshold of
\(5\times10^{-8}\). Begin with the strongest effect and a target of 90%
power. Kim describes the effect in odds-ratio language. To reproduce this
design the package uses the numerical value 2 as its one-copy relative risk
`R1` in a multiplicative transmission model, with two-copy relative risk
`R2 = R1^2`. An odds ratio from a different study needs its own risk-model
justification.

```{r kim-ais-replication}
kim_4x <- tdt_ngs_mssn(
  power = 0.90,
  pd = 0.35,
  R1 = 2,
  coverage = 4,
  seq_error = 0.025,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  verbose = FALSE
)

kim_25x <- tdt_ngs_mssn(
  power = 0.90,
  pd = 0.35,
  R1 = 2,
  coverage = 25,
  seq_error = 0.025,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r kim-ais-replication-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  coverage = c("4x", "25x"),
  published_trios = c(654, 416),
  paweh_trios = c(kim_4x$MSSN_trios, kim_25x$MSSN_trios)
), digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Depth", "Paper (trios)", "Calculated (trios)"),
  caption = "Published and calculated recruitment for 90% power in the AIS design.")
```

Moving from 4× to 25× reduces the target from **654 to 416 complete
trios**, or from 1,962 to 1,248 people. More reads help distinguish plausible
parent–child genotype patterns. Each trio then contributes more information
about transmission. A team assessing cost would need prices for both
recruitment and sequencing to compare the two plans.

The remaining designs change the effect size **and** the desired power.
Each pair of rows holds both fixed while changing depth. The comparison
column contains the six Table 3 benchmarks.

```{r kim-table-3}
kim_table3 <- data.frame(
  coverage = rep(c(4, 25), times = 3),
  power = rep(c(0.90, 0.70, 0.10), each = 2),
  R1 = rep(c(2.0, 1.8, 1.5), each = 2),
  published_trios = c(654, 416, 716, 456, 733, 466)
)

kim_table3$paweh_trios <- c(
  kim_4x$MSSN_trios,
  kim_25x$MSSN_trios,
  vapply(3:6, function(i) {
    tdt_ngs_mssn(
      power = kim_table3$power[i], pd = 0.35, R1 = kim_table3$R1[i],
      coverage = kim_table3$coverage[i], seq_error = 0.025,
      alpha = 5e-8, verbose = FALSE
    )$MSSN_trios
  }, numeric(1))
)
```

```{r kim-table-3-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(kim_table3[, c("coverage", "power", "R1", "published_trios", "paweh_trios")], digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Depth", "Target power", "R1", "Table 3 trios", "Calculated trios"),
  caption = "Kim Table 3 benchmarks and calculated complete trios for three designs.")
```

All six calculated integers match. For effect 1.8 and 70% target power
the counts are 716 and 456. For effect 1.5 and 10% target power they are
733 and 466. The last design would detect only about one in ten associations
of its proposed size. It illustrates the published calculation, rather
than a conventional recruitment target.

## Plan a study with 5,000 families available

Suppose the team expects a smaller genetic effect than in the first AIS
example. The following assumptions use a setting from the design grid in
Gordon, Finch, and Kim (2020, §5.4.4).

| Input | Value | Interpretation |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `N` | 5,000 | Complete, independent trios available for a power calculation. |
| `power` | 0.80 | Target for the separate MSSN calculation. |
| `pd` | 0.325 | Population frequency of the designated allele in the parental model. |
| `R1` | 1.2 | Disease risk with one copy relative to zero copies. The implied two-copy relative risk is 1.44. |
| `coverage` | 12 | Each parent's and child's fixed read depth at this site. |
| `seq_error` | 0.005 | Probability a read of either allele is reported as the other one. |
| `alpha` | 5e-8 | Nominal significance threshold for the transmission test. |

Table: Inputs for fixed-sample power and minimum recruitment under TDT1-NGS.

Use `tdt_ngs_power()` for the available families and `tdt_ngs_mssn()`
to solve for the target. Both calls use the same multiplicative model.

```{r tdt-ngs-workflow}
tdt_seq_power <- tdt_ngs_power(
  N = 5000,
  pd = 0.325,
  R1 = 1.2,
  coverage = 12,
  seq_error = 0.005,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  verbose = FALSE
)

tdt_seq_mssn <- tdt_ngs_mssn(
  power = 0.80,
  pd = 0.325,
  R1 = 1.2,
  coverage = 12,
  seq_error = 0.005,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r tdt-ngs-workflow-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("Power at 5,000 trios", "Required trios", "Total individuals"),
  value = c(
    sprintf("%.5f", tdt_seq_power$power),
    tdt_seq_mssn$MSSN_trios,
    tdt_seq_mssn$total_individuals
  )
), digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Design quantity", "Value"),
  caption = "Read-count design at 12× for a fixed budget and an 80% target.")
```

At 12×, **5,000 trios give 70.73% power**. For 80% power, plan for **5,507
complete trios**, or **16,521 individuals**. The whole-trio design achieves
80.014% power. If 5,000 families is a firm ceiling, the coverage curves
below show what additional reads can buy under these assumptions.

### Advanced detail: the information in a trio

For each possible father, mother and child genotype, the likelihood gives
the probability of their three read counts. Summing over the 15 genetically
possible ordered trio states, weighted by their model probabilities, retains
evidence from families whose genotypes are ambiguous. The transmission
probability from an informative parent in this model is
\(t=R_1/(1+R_1)\). Equal transmission under the null gives \(t=1/2\).

Kim's Appendix B gives the design noncentrality parameter (NCP), the
quantity used to predict separation from the null:

\[
\lambda=N\{\log R_1\}^2 I_{\mathrm{eff}}.
\]

Here \(I_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is the per-trio information under the null after
allowing for nuisance parameters, including parental mating frequencies
and read errors. The calculation compares the resulting noncentral
chi-square distribution to the central one-degree-of-freedom cutoff. For
MSSN it solves for the target NCP and rounds up to a complete family.

## How sensitive is the result to who enters the family study?

A child enrolled as affected might have been misclassified. Alternatively,
some correctly diagnosed families might have disease unrelated to the locus
under study. The following settings extend the basic trio design.

| Argument | Example value | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `pheno_misclass`, `prev`, `pi01` | TRUE, 0.01, 0.05 | Switch on the diagnosis sensitivity, supply true prevalence and the false-positive probability among unaffected children. |
| `locus_het`, `heter_rate` | TRUE, 0.25 | Switch on the independent sensitivity to the fraction of families unlinked to the locus. It also requires prevalence. |
| `father_coverage`, `mother_coverage`, `child_coverage` | 6, 12, 20 | Override the shared read depth by family role. |
| `epsilon0`, `epsilon1` | 0.005, 0.015 | Set reference-to-alternate and alternate-to-reference read-error probabilities, respectively. |

Table: Optional inputs for changing the trio ascertainment or sequencing assumptions.

In the first scenario `prev = 0.01` is the true population
prevalence and `pi01 = 0.05` is the probability of classifying a truly
unaffected child as affected. With many more unaffected than affected
children, even a modest false-positive rate can strongly dilute the
transmission signal.

```{r tdt-ngs-phenotype-misclassification}
tdt_pheno <- tdt_ngs_power(
  N = 5000, pd = 0.325, R1 = 1.2,
  coverage = 12, seq_error = 0.005,
  pheno_misclass = TRUE, prev = 0.01, pi01 = 0.05,
  alpha = 5e-8, verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r tdt-ngs-phenotype-misclassification-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(tdt_pheno$scenarios),
  NCP = vapply(tdt_pheno$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "lambda"),
  Power = vapply(tdt_pheno$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "power"),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = c(0, 4, 8), caption = "Power under sequencing alone and in the diagnosis sensitivity.")
```

In the 5,000-trio design, this sensitivity calculation drops power from
0.7073 to about **0.00000372**. That last value is a probability, well below
0.01%. Now consider a different concern: `heter_rate = 0.25` assigns a
quarter of families to an unlinked component, leaving 75% linked. Both
sensitivities require `prev`; the sequencing-only calculation does not
use prevalence.

```{r tdt-ngs-locus-heterogeneity}
tdt_het <- tdt_ngs_power(
  N = 5000, pd = 0.325, R1 = 1.2,
  coverage = 12, seq_error = 0.005,
  locus_het = TRUE, prev = 0.01, heter_rate = 0.25,
  alpha = 5e-8, verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r tdt-ngs-locus-heterogeneity-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(tdt_het$scenarios),
  NCP = vapply(tdt_het$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "lambda"),
  Power = vapply(tdt_het$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "power"),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = c(0, 4, 8), caption = "Power when one quarter of trios are unlinked.")
```

With one quarter unlinked, power is **17.01%**. Requesting both modifiers
returns each comparison against the original 70.73% sequencing baseline.
There is no jointly fitted phenotype-error and heterogeneity model.

**How the sensitivities are calculated.** The package obtains an attenuation
factor from the ordinary TDT. Its per-trio coefficient is
\(c=2(g_T-g_{NT})^2/(g_T+g_{NT})\), using the probabilities of informative
transmission and non-transmission. It calculates \(c\) with and without
one modifier and multiplies the sequencing NCP by their ratio. The ordinary
models use \(R_2=R_1^2\), maximal positive LD (\(D'=1\)) and a linked-family
recombination parameter fixed numerically at \(\theta_1=p_d\). For
heterogeneity, the linked fraction is \(1-\mathrm{heter\_rate}\).
The ordinary-TDT equations are described in §§5.2.6 and 5.3.3 of the
textbook. Applying their ratio to Kim's NCP is a package extension.
Kim's read-count likelihood and its efficient information remain the
sequencing-only quantities for each scenario. The result object records
the coefficients and assumptions in each scenario's `ordinary_tdt_bridge`.

## What if family members have different depths or read errors are directional?

Use `father_coverage`, `mother_coverage` and `child_coverage` to give each
family role its own depth. An omitted member setting inherits `coverage`.
`epsilon0` is the probability of reading reference as alternate, and
`epsilon1` is the probability of reading alternate as reference. Each
inherits `seq_error` unless supplied. The pair is shared across family
members. Each directional probability must be nonnegative and their sum
must be below one. In this example fathers have six reads, mothers twelve,
and children twenty.

```{r tdt-ngs-member-sequencing}
tdt_member_specific <- tdt_ngs_power(
  N = 5000, pd = 0.325, R1 = 1.2,
  father_coverage = 6, mother_coverage = 12, child_coverage = 20,
  epsilon0 = 0.005, epsilon1 = 0.015,
  alpha = 5e-8, verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r tdt-ngs-member-sequencing-result, echo=FALSE}
tdt_member_specific$power
```

The proposed allocation and directional errors give **68.12% power** at
5,000 trios. Both depth and error assumptions changed from the earlier
example, so their individual effects cannot be isolated from this comparison.
For a genotype with \(G\) alternate copies, the alternate-read probability is

\[
q_G=\epsilon_0+(1-\epsilon_0-\epsilon_1)G/2.
\]

The three probabilities here are 0.005, 0.495 and 0.985. Errors in opposite
directions balance for a heterozygote when the two rates are equal.

## What does deeper sequencing buy at fixed risk and allele frequency?

The first plot varies the common depth on the horizontal axis at **5,000
trios**. Each line assumes a different symmetric per-read error rate.
Allele frequency, risk and significance threshold are the same as in the
12× example. The horizontal reference is the desired power of 0.80.

```{r tdt-ngs-power-plot, fig.cap="TDT1-NGS power across equal fixed coverage for two symmetric per-read error assumptions."}
plot_ngs_power(
  design = "tdt",
  coverage = c(2, 4, 8, 12, 20),
  seq_error = c(0.005, 0.01),
  target_power = 0.80,
  N = 5000, pd = 0.325, R1 = 1.2, alpha = 5e-8
)
```

At 0.005 error, power rises from **42.31% at 4× to 70.73% at 12×**, then
to 72.04% at 20×. Ambiguous families become easier to distinguish with the
first additional reads. Once their inheritance pattern is already well
supported, more reads add less information. Neither error curve reaches
80% on this depth grid.

Now hold the target at 80% and ask how many complete trios each depth and
error rate requires. The other biological assumptions stay fixed.

```{r tdt-ngs-mssn-plot, fig.cap="Required complete trios across equal fixed coverage for two symmetric per-read error assumptions."}
plot_ngs_mssn(
  design = "tdt",
  coverage = c(2, 4, 8, 12, 20),
  seq_error = c(0.005, 0.01),
  power = 0.80, pd = 0.325, R1 = 1.2, alpha = 5e-8
)
```

At 0.005 error, increasing depth from 4× to 12× saves **1,657 trios**
(7,164 to 5,507). Increasing it from 12× to 20× saves another 71. The lines
compare planned experiments at specified error rates. They give neither
a confidence interval nor an optimal spending allocation. The implementation
requires at least two reads for **each** member. At 1× it cannot identify
the efficient information under its full nuisance-parameter model. This
restriction is specific to the implemented TDT1-NGS calculation.

# Unrelated cases and controls: from reads to genotype scores

Suppose the team can recruit people who meet the disease definition and
unrelated controls from the same source population. It will test whether
the average genotype score differs between the groups. To plan that study,
we need to know how often sequencing would put a person into each of the
three score categories.

## Read a genotype-calling matrix

Return to the matrix from the opening example, this time allowing 0.5% error
per read. The next call gives the three possible **called** genotypes across
the columns for each **true** genotype down the rows.

```{r cc-transition-matrix}
ngs_genotype_error_matrix(coverage = 4, seq_error = 0.005)
```

At 4× a true heterozygote is called correctly 87.5% of the time. It is
called a reference homozygote 6.25% of the time and an alternate homozygote
6.25% of the time. A true reference homozygote has about a 1.99% chance
of a heterozygous call. Each row sums to one because every possible read
count is assigned to one of the three genotypes.

For a fixed depth \(v\) and symmetric base-call error \(e\), the number
\(X\) of alternate reads is binomial:

\[
 X\mid G=g \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(v,q_g),\qquad
 (q_0,q_1,q_2)=(e,\;1/2,\;1-e).
\]

For each possible count from 0 to \(v\), the caller selects the genotype that
makes that count most likely, using a deterministic rule for ties. Summing
the probabilities of counts assigned to each call gives the transition
matrix \(E\). Depth changes the number and concentration of possible counts.
Base-call error changes their probabilities even at the same depth. If
\(g\) is a column of true genotype proportions in a group, \(E^{\mathsf T}g\)
gives the called proportions. This transformation is applied separately
to cases and controls before calculating the difference in their mean scores.

## Where does the trend-test calculation come from?

Chapman and Nam (1968) derived asymptotic power for a test of linear trend.
Ahn et al. (2007, Eq. 1) applied it to SNP genotype scores in unrelated
cases and controls. A SNP is a variant at a single DNA position. Ahn's
question was how errors in an already assigned genotype change power. The
paper specified genotype-error probabilities directly.

Their worked comparison (p. 257) used risk and marker allele frequencies
of 0.30, prevalence 0.005, normalized LD of 0.5, and one- and two-copy
relative risks of 2 and 3. The two frequency vectors below are the resulting
reconstructed marker genotype proportions for cases and controls, ordered
by number of copies. Compare 1,000 people per group at `alpha = 0.001`.
The scores `w = c(0, 1, 2)` count copies. The two-degree-of-freedom
genotype test instead compares all three category proportions. The
`3p` settings allow 5% for each adjacent transition and zero for a jump
between opposite homozygotes.

```{r ahn-published-method-replication}
ahn_case <- c(0.398125, 0.472500, 0.129375)
ahn_control <- c(0.490461683417085, 0.419736180904523, 0.089802135678392)

ahn_no_error <- cc_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.001,
  input_mode = "model_free",
  g1 = ahn_case, g0 = ahn_control,
  k = 1, w = c(0, 1, 2),
  geno_misclass = "none", verbose = FALSE
)

ahn_adjacent_error <- cc_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.001,
  input_mode = "model_free",
  g1 = ahn_case, g0 = ahn_control,
  k = 1, w = c(0, 1, 2),
  geno_misclass = "3p", e01 = 0.05, e02 = 0.05, e03 = 0,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r ahn-published-method-replication-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  scenario = c("No error", "No error", "5% adjacent error", "5% adjacent error"),
  test = c("T012", "Genotype chi-square", "T012", "Genotype chi-square"),
  published_approximate_power = c(0.88, 0.81, 0.79, 0.70),
  paweh_power = c(
    ahn_no_error$tests$trend$power,
    ahn_no_error$tests$genotypes$power,
    ahn_adjacent_error$tests$trend$power,
    ahn_adjacent_error$tests$genotypes$power
  )
), digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Calling scenario", "Test", "Paper", "Calculated"),
  caption = "Ordinary genotype error in the Ahn example, with the published approximate and computed powers.")
```

The trend test gives **0.8743 and 0.7876** power with accurate calls and
adjacent errors, respectively. The genotype test gives **0.8061 and
0.6992**. Ahn reports approximately 0.88 and 0.79 for trend and 0.81 and
0.70 for the genotype test. The comparison reproduces the published method
and closely matches the reported powers. These calls take genotype
frequencies and conventional error rates directly. The upstream conversion
from sequencing depth and per-read error to a calling matrix is a
`paweh` composition.

## Would 1,000 cases and 1,000 controls suffice?

Here the genotype proportions come from a disease model. Use these
assumptions to plan a test at a stringent significance level.

| Input | Choice | Meaning in the case-control design |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `N_case`, `k` | 1,000, 1 | Available cases and controls per case. Equal allocation gives 2,000 people. |
| `alpha`, `power` | 5e-8, 0.80 | Nominal test threshold and target for the sample-size calculation. |
| `pd`, `prev` | 0.30, 0.05 | Risk-allele frequency and disease prevalence in the source population. Prevalence anchors absolute genotype risks. |
| `R2` | 1.8 | Risk with two copies relative to zero. |
| `MOI` | `"M"` | Multiplicative mode of inheritance. The implied one-copy risk ratio is `sqrt(1.8)` and trend scores are 0, 1, 2. |
| `coverage`, `seq_error` | 4, 0.005 | Four reads per person with symmetric 0.5% error per read. Depth is a positive integer and symmetric error is in [0, 0.5). |

Table: Inputs for a case-control power calculation and its inverse.

The case-control functions derive one-copy risk from `R2` and `MOI`.
For dominant inheritance (`"D"`) both carriers have risk ratio `R2`
and scores are 0, 1, 1. For recessive inheritance (`"Rec"`) the one-copy
risk ratio is 1 and scores are 0, 0, 1. The baseline population follows
HWE. The model uses genotype-specific disease risks to determine which
genotypes are expected among cases and controls, and then applies the
calling matrix.

```{r cc-ngs-workflow}
cc_seq_power <- cc_ngs_power(
  N_case = 1000,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  prev = 0.05,
  pd = 0.30,
  R2 = 1.8,
  coverage = 4,
  seq_error = 0.005,
  MOI = "M",
  k = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)

cc_seq_mssn <- cc_ngs_mssn(
  power = 0.80,
  alpha = 5e-8,
  prev = 0.05,
  pd = 0.30,
  R2 = 1.8,
  coverage = 4,
  seq_error = 0.005,
  MOI = "M",
  k = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-workflow-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Power at 1,000 cases", "Required cases", "Required controls", "Total MSSN"
  ),
  value = c(
    sprintf("%.5f", cc_seq_power$power),
    cc_seq_mssn$MSSN_case,
    cc_seq_mssn$MSSN_ctrl,
    cc_seq_mssn$MSSN_total
  )
), digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Design quantity", "Value"),
  caption = "Case-control trend power at the available budget and recruitment for 80% power.")
```

At 4× the proposed 2,000-person sample gives **11.97% power**. The
80% design calls for **2,168 cases and 2,168 controls**, or **4,336
people**. Its achieved power is 80.04%. The sample-size calculation
solves the trend-test equation, then checks the integer allocation.

## How much does depth change case-control recruitment?

First fix the original 1,000 cases and 1,000 controls. The horizontal axis
varies depth in both groups, while the two lines represent 0.5% and 1%
symmetric error. The vertical axis gives power for the same multiplicative
risk, frequency, prevalence and significance threshold.

```{r cc-ngs-power-plot, fig.cap="Case-control sequencing trend power across equal fixed coverage for two symmetric per-read error assumptions."}
plot_ngs_power(
  design = "cc",
  coverage = c(2, 4, 8, 12, 20),
  seq_error = c(0.005, 0.01),
  target_power = 0.80,
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 5e-8,
  prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8, MOI = "M", k = 1
)
```

At 0.5% error the power rises from 11.97% at 4× to 19.01% at 12× and
19.50% at 20×. More depth reduces ambiguity in genotype scores, but even
20× leaves this recruitment plan far below its 80% target. The lines do
not estimate how an actual laboratory's error rate changes with depth.

Now solve for recruitment at each of the same depths, with the same two
error rates. This plot's vertical axis counts **cases**. The plan still
requires one control for each case.

```{r cc-ngs-mssn-plot, fig.cap="Required case sample size across equal fixed coverage for two symmetric per-read error assumptions."}
plot_ngs_mssn(
  design = "cc",
  coverage = c(2, 4, 8, 12, 20),
  seq_error = c(0.005, 0.01),
  power = 0.80, alpha = 5e-8,
  prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8, MOI = "M", k = 1
)
```

At 0.5% error, the requirement falls from 2,168 cases at 4× to 1,893 at
12× and 1,879 at 20×. Most of the savings here occur before 12×. The
points summarize the chosen caller and grid. A cost comparison also needs
the cost per person and per read.

# What if cases and controls are measured differently?

A case series sequenced today and an older control collection might have
different depths or error rates. Supply `case_coverage` and `ctrl_coverage`
for separate depths and `case_seq_error` and `ctrl_seq_error` for separate
symmetric read errors. A group-specific argument overrides the common
value for that group. This example also changes the significance level to
0.05, so compare the scenarios **within** this example.

```{r cc-ngs-differential}
cc_differential <- cc_ngs_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.05, prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8,
  coverage = 10, seq_error = 0.01,
  case_coverage = 4, case_seq_error = 0.04,
  locus_het = TRUE, pi = 0.75, verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-differential-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(cc_differential$scenarios),
  NCP = vapply(cc_differential$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "lambda"),
  Power = vapply(cc_differential$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "power"),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = c(0, 4, 8), caption = "Nominal power with different sequencing in cases and controls.")
```

Here cases use 4× and 4% error, while controls inherit 10× and 1% error.
The sequencing-only nominal power is 0.99995. In a separate heterogeneity
scenario, `pi = 0.75` keeps 75% of cases from the locus-associated
distribution and mixes in 25% from the control distribution before
sequencing. The nominal power becomes 0.99846.

A mistaken diagnosis acts at another stage. Set `theta = 0.02` to label
2% of true cases as controls and `phi = 0.01` to label 1% of true controls
as cases. The package uses prevalence to work out the genotype mix in each
observed disease group before applying that group's sequencing model.

```{r cc-ngs-phenotype-misclassification}
cc_pheno_differential <- cc_ngs_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.05, prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8,
  coverage = 10, seq_error = 0.01,
  case_coverage = 4, case_seq_error = 0.04,
  locus_het = TRUE, pi = 0.75,
  pheno_misclass = TRUE, theta = 0.02, phi = 0.01,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-phenotype-misclassification-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(cc_pheno_differential$scenarios),
  NCP = vapply(cc_pheno_differential$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "lambda"),
  Power = vapply(cc_pheno_differential$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "power"),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = c(0, 4, 8), caption = "Separate comparisons with diagnosis error and heterogeneity.")
```

The phenotype scenario gives nominal power 0.99949. This call also requests
heterogeneity, so its result contains two distinct comparisons against
sequencing alone. Read the named `scenarios` entries when comparing several
design assumptions.

Finally, consider a conventional genotype error **after** the sequencing
caller has assigned a genotype. The package supports common one-, two- and
three-parameter models (`"1p"`, `"2p"`, `"3p"`) or separate three-parameter
matrices (`"diff3p"`). In the latter, each group's `e01` gives the chance
a called homozygote becomes a heterozygote, `e02` the chance a called
heterozygote becomes *each* homozygote, and `e03` the chance of switching
between homozygotes. The example requests all three sensitivities.

```{r cc-ngs-genotype-misclassification}
cc_all_errors <- cc_ngs_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.05, prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8,
  case_coverage = 4, ctrl_coverage = 10,
  case_seq_error = 0.04, ctrl_seq_error = 0.01,
  locus_het = TRUE, pi = 0.75,
  pheno_misclass = TRUE, theta = 0.02, phi = 0.01,
  geno_misclass = "diff3p",
  case_e01 = 0.03, case_e02 = 0.01, case_e03 = 0.004,
  ctrl_e01 = 0.01, ctrl_e02 = 0.005, ctrl_e03 = 0.002,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-genotype-misclassification-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = names(cc_all_errors$scenarios),
  NCP = vapply(cc_all_errors$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "lambda"),
  Power = vapply(cc_all_errors$scenarios, `[[`, numeric(1), "power"),
  row.names = NULL
), digits = c(0, 4, 8), caption = "Nominal power for each requested scenario at the 0.05 cutoff.")
```

Each row uses the same sequencing design. In the phenotype and heterogeneity
rows the biological mixture changes **before** sequencing. The genotype-error
row starts with the original biological groups and transforms their
sequencing calls **afterward**. For each group its effective transition
matrix in row notation is \(E_{\rm sequencing}E_{\rm genotype}\).
The three modifiers each act on their own and there is no combined
all-errors result.

Notice that nominal power rises slightly in the genotype-error row.
Different observation processes can create a score difference even when
there is no biological association. These calculations retain the nominal
chi-square cutoff. A large rejection probability under differential error
does not establish that the test controls its Type I error at `alpha`.
For an audit, `sequencing` holds the two calling matrices, `freqs` records
intermediate and final group frequencies, and the relevant scenario's
`errors` component records the additional error model.

## When does increasing recruitment stop helping?

With the same 4× sequencing mechanism in both groups, we can isolate the
effect of locus heterogeneity. The case distribution before sequencing is
\(\pi g_{\rm case}+(1-\pi)g_{\rm control}\). Here `pi` is the fraction
retaining the locus-specific case distribution. In the trio interface
`heter_rate` counts the **unlinked** fraction instead.

```{r cc-ngs-heterogeneity}
cc_heterogeneous <- cc_ngs_power(
  N_case = 1000, alpha = 0.05,
  prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8,
  coverage = 4, seq_error = 0.005,
  MOI = "M", k = 1,
  locus_het = TRUE, pi = 0.75,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-heterogeneity-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  pi = cc_heterogeneous$locus_het$pi,
  lambda = cc_heterogeneous$lambda,
  power = cc_heterogeneous$power
), digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Associated fraction", "NCP", "Power"),
  caption = "Heterogeneity scenario with equal sequencing in cases and controls.")
```

At the 0.05 cutoff, 75% locus-associated cases give 89.75% power and an
NCP of 10.42. With identical measurement processes and `pi = 0`, cases
and controls have identical called genotype distributions. The trend
contrast vanishes, its NCP is zero and power equals the nominal level.
Use the plotting function's data output to see how the sample-size
calculation represents that limit.

```{r cc-ngs-null-boundary}
pi_boundary <- plot_ngs_mssn(
  design = "cc",
  coverage = 4,
  seq_error = 0.005,
  return_data = TRUE,
  power = 0.80, alpha = 0.05,
  prev = 0.05, pd = 0.30, R2 = 1.8, MOI = "M", k = 1,
  locus_het = TRUE, pi = c(1, 0.75, 0.50, 0)
)
```

```{r cc-ngs-null-boundary-result, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(pi_boundary[, c("pi", "MSSN_case", "finite_mssn", "status")], digits = 5,
  col.names = c("Associated fraction", "Cases", "Finite MSSN", "Status"),
  caption = "Case recruitment as the fraction of locus-associated cases decreases.")
```

For 80% power the requirements rise from 430 to 754 to 1,671 cases as
`pi` falls from 1 to 0.75 to 0.50. At zero, `finite_mssn = FALSE` and
the missing count means **no finite MSSN**. This conclusion requires an
observed contrast of zero. Differential sequencing can produce different
called distributions from identical biological groups, so `pi = 0` by
itself cannot establish that boundary for every design.

# Fixed depths, study units and a recruitment decision

The comparison below summarizes the assumptions needed to report either
design. Real data may include sites with no reads and others with many reads
in the same person. Entering an average depth applies one fixed value to
everyone in that group or family role. These functions do not integrate
over an empirical distribution of depths. In particular, averaging depths
before a nonlinear power calculation can give a different result from
modeling the individual depths.

| Assumption | Case-control NGS | TDT1-NGS |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Locus and sampling | Single biallelic locus in unrelated cases and controls | Single biallelic locus in complete affected-child trios |
| Population and inheritance | HWE source frequencies with multiplicative, dominant or recessive risk and scores | Parental HWE, random mating, Mendelian transmission and multiplicative risk |
| Coverage | Fixed per group, at least 1× | Fixed per family role, at least 2× |
| Base-call error | Symmetric per group, possibly differential between groups | Common directional pair across family roles |
| Evidence in the test | Deterministic genotype calls and case-control trend scores | Likelihood of the family's read counts across possible genotypes |
| Locus heterogeneity | Mix case and control genotype frequencies | Ordinary-TDT NCP attenuation |
| Phenotype misclassification | Prevalence-weighted mixture of biological groups | Separate ordinary-TDT NCP attenuation |
| Additional conventional genotype errors | Common or group-specific matrices after sequencing | Outside the raw-read design |
| Computation | Analytic with finite sums | Analytic with finite sums |

Table: Assumptions and units for the two prospective sequencing designs.

1. **Start with who you can recruit.** For unrelated cases and controls,
   use `cc_ngs_power()` with the available case count and control/case ratio.
   For families, use `tdt_ngs_power()` with the number of complete trios.
2. **Write down how the effect and reads are modeled.** Record the allele
   frequency, inheritance model, risk ratio, nominal significance level,
   depth and per-read error. Case-control plans also need prevalence and
   allocation. State any group-specific or member-specific differences.
3. **Solve for recruitment.** Use the matching `*_mssn()` function with
   the desired power. Report cases **and** controls for a case-control design,
   or complete trios and their participant equivalent for a family design.
4. **Check which assumption changes the decision.** Vary depth and read
   error over plausible ranges. If case definitions or genetic causes vary,
   report each sensitivity against its sequencing-only baseline. Compare
   the resulting recruitment and sequencing workloads with the actual budget.

# Methods and references

Kim's Table 3 provides the family benchmark and Appendix B the TDT1-NGS
information calculation. Ahn et al. provide the ordinary genotype-error
comparison and apply the Chapman–Nam trend method. The sequencing-to-call
matrix and its composition with that trend method are package calculations.
In the textbook, §§2.6.1–2.6.2 introduce the read model, §4.4.2 discusses
TDT1-NGS, and §5.4.4 studies its power. The raw-read case-control test
LTTae,NGS in §§4.4.1 and 5.4.1–5.4.3 is a different procedure.

Ahn K, Haynes C, Kim W, St Fleur R, Gordon D, Finch SJ. The effects of SNP
genotyping errors on the power of the Cochran-Armitage linear trend test for
case/control association studies. *Annals of Human Genetics*.
2007;71(2):249--261.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-1809.2006.00318.x>.

Chapman DG, Nam JM. Asymptotic power of chi square tests for linear trends in
proportions. *Biometrics*. 1968;24(2):315--327.
<https://doi.org/10.2307/2528035>.

Gordon D, Finch SJ, Kim W. *Heterogeneity in Statistical Genetics: How to
Assess, Address, and Account for Mixtures in Association Studies*. Springer;
2020. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-61121-7>.

Kim W. Transmission disequilibrium tests based on read counts for low-coverage
next-generation sequence data. *Human Heredity*. 2015;80(1):36--49.
<https://doi.org/10.1159/000434645>.
